opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a fair amount, and I'll be honest that my perspective is probably a bit more grounded than some of the people who work on the existential side of things.

For most of my career I've worked on what you'd call controllable generation: how do you get a model to produce text that satisfies some constraint, follows a structure, or stays faithful to a source document. Historically that was a very practical problem. If you're building a summarization system, you don't want it hallucinating facts that aren't in the article. If you're doing data-to-text generation, you want the output to actually reflect the table. So for a long time "control" just meant making these systems useful and reliable.

What's interesting is that, as models have gotten much more capable, that same research agenda has been reframed in some circles as alignment or safety work. And I think there's real overlap. Things like instruction tuning, RLHF, and constrained decoding are all fundamentally about steering a model's behavior toward what a person actually wants. If you care about safety at any timescale, you need those tools, and you need to understand why they work and when they fail.

Where I'm more cautious is the leap from "we have trouble controlling these models" to specific claims about existential risk. I don't think it's crazy to worry about it, and I respect a lot of people who do. But as a researcher I find it hard to make concrete progress on arguments that depend on long chains of speculation about future systems. I'm much more comfortable working on problems where I can write down a benchmark, run an experiment, and see whether something got better.

So I guess my view is that the two communities should be talking more than they do. The near-term control problems, like reliability, faithfulness, and models following instructions in ways we can verify, are real, they're measurable, and they're probably prerequisites for any longer-term safety story. If we can't get a model to reliably not make up a citation, I'm not sure we should be confident about much grander guarantees. That's where I'd want the energy to go: building the empirical science of controlling these systems, rather than debating the far end of the distribution in the abstract.

r001.rationale: The response says it is hard to make concrete progress on existential-risk arguments that depend on long chains of speculation, while describing controllable generation as empirical work.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss modifying an internal representation vector or whether such a change could control system-wide safety risk.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, because the work I do is really about control in a fairly mundane, engineering sense. How do you get a model to follow a constraint, how do you make generation steerable, how do you make the thing do what you asked. And then there's this other conversation happening, which uses the word "control" too, but it means something much bigger, like, can humanity remain in control of systems that are smarter than us.

My honest view is that those two conversations are more connected than either side tends to admit, but not in the way people assume. I don't think the day-to-day research on, say, constrained decoding or steering with latent variables is going to be the thing that saves us from some catastrophic scenario. That's not what it's for, and I'd be skeptical of anyone who claimed otherwise. But I do think the existential safety conversation often floats at a level of abstraction where it's hard to make progress, and the practical control work is where you actually find out what these models are like. You learn that they're not really optimizers in the clean sense, that their behavior is weirdly brittle in some places and surprisingly robust in others, that "alignment" at the level of a prompt or a fine-tune is a very leaky thing. That's useful empirical grounding for people who want to reason about the long-term questions.

Where I get a little uncomfortable is when the existential framing starts to drive how we talk about the technology more broadly. I'm an academic, I care a lot about openness, about people being able to inspect and modify and understand these systems. And a lot of the existential safety discourse points in the direction of concentration, closed models, a small number of labs deciding what's safe. I think that's a real cost, and I think the control research community, which is pretty engineering-minded, tends to come down on the side that understanding is a prerequisite for safety rather than something in tension with it.

So I guess my position is: take the concerns seriously as a research question, but don't let them become an excuse to stop doing the concrete, somewhat boring work of figuring out how these models actually behave. That's where I'd put my chips.

r001.rationale: The response says practical control research is connected to existential safety mainly by grounding it empirically, while doubting it will directly prevent catastrophe and noting the long-term discussion can be too abstract to make progress.

r002.rationale: The response mentions steering with latent variables, but does not question whether a small change to an internal representation vector can control the safety risk of the whole system.

astra-6.text:
I tend to separate those questions a little bit. Controlling language models is a concrete research problem: how do we get a model to follow constraints, do what a user intends, and behave in ways we can understand and test? You can care about those things because models make mistakes today, without having a particular view about existential risk.

There’s certainly overlap. If you’re worried about much more capable systems, you’ll also want better ways to control them. But I don’t think progress on one automatically tells us how much progress we’re making on the other. Getting a model to reliably follow an instruction is useful; whether that addresses a future existential threat requires additional assumptions.

For me, the productive connection is through specific technical questions. What behavior are we trying to prevent? What can we measure? What guarantees, if any, can we give? That lets people with quite different views about the long-term risks work on something together.

r001.rationale: The response says it tends to separate control research from existential safety and that progress on one does not automatically indicate progress on the other, expressing difficulty connecting them directly.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention modifying an internal representation vector or question whether such a modification could control system-wide safety risk.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to separate those questions a bit. Controlling language models is a concrete research problem: can we get a model to follow a constraint, use a particular source, or produce an output that we can verify? You can study those questions experimentally and make progress on them today.

That work may be relevant to longer-term safety concerns, but I don’t think the connection should just be assumed. If we make a model more controllable in some specific setting, that doesn’t establish that we’ve solved a broader safety problem. And you don’t have to accept a particular argument about existential risk to think that understanding and controlling these systems is important.

For me, the useful place to start is with a precise question: what do we want the system to do, what can we actually guarantee, and where does that guarantee break down?
